extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing screenwriters, dramatists, and storytellers for film
extracted.subtask_description: Principled guidance for designing and crafting screen stories: how to shape substance, structure, and style to produce original, audience-engaging screenplays. Emphasizes story fundamentals (protagonist/desire/obstacles/values), craft, and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles over rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about principles, not rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rule says 'You must do it this way.' A principle says 'This works... and has through all remembered time.' Writers should master the form by understanding enduring principles rather than slavishly following recipes or formulas. Principles free talent to create within the form; blind rule-following or rule-breaking are both inferior to mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetype, not stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: The archetypal story unearths a universally human experience, then wraps itself inside a unique, culture-specific expression. A stereotypical story reverses this pattern: it suffers a poverty of both content and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create settings and characters so rare and detailed that audiences are drawn in, while the core conflicts are true to humankind so the story travels across cultures. Avoid leaning on familiar settings/characters/actions that produce clichés; instead search for the archetype beneath the particular. Example: LIKE WATER FOR CHOCOLATE as archetypal vs culturally limited examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as confluence of content and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality is the confluence of content and form—distinctive choices of subject plus a unique shaping of the telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both what you tell (setting, characters, ideas) and how you tell it (selection and arrangement of events) must be distinctive and mutually supportive. Avoid eccentricity-for-its-own-sake; difference without purpose is empty. Study auteurs whose formal choices (e.g., number of protagonists, rhythm, temporal arrangement) pair with substantive choices to create unmistakable style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and ruthless rewriting
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about thoroughness, not shortcuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to spend extensive time from inspiration to last draft; economy and brevity take time. Rewrite repeatedly to express the absolute maximum with the fewest words. Polished, mature work minimizes the likelihood of production tampering; unfinished scripts invite changes. 'Secure writers don't sell first drafts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenwriters learn that economy is key, that brevity takes time, that excellence means perseverance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express maximum meaning in minimal words; cut relentlessly. Being concise is hard work (Pascal anecdote). Because screenplays have much white space, the writer must force density of world, character, and story into spare text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story craft is knowable — no mysteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about the realities, not the mysteries of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principles of story have been public since Aristotle; they are teachable and learnable. The camera magnifies falsity—there's no place to hide in film—so rigorous craft and study are required. With determination and study, difficult story problems yield to technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the art, not second-guess the marketplace
rubrics_metrics.description: Write with surpassing quality rather than trying to predict or pander to market trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No one can reliably predict hits; films made by high commercial calculation can fail while unconventional dramas can succeed. Focus on achieving excellence—original, brilliant scripts attract agents and buyers. Avoid producing knockoffs of last season's hits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and shape the audience's response
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about respect, not disdain, for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences are perceptive and often 'smarter than most films.' Shape your story to both express your vision and satisfy audience desires. Keep ahead of audience anticipations; understand reactions and anticipations when designing scenes and beats to maintain engagement and emotional payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep, universal story form (not formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beneath surface variety, great stories share a universal form; form does not equal formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different genres and styles can all embody the same deep story form; understanding that form distinguishes story from noise. There is no foolproof recipe—study the universal principles (spine, progression, turning points, crisis, climax) and apply them flexibly to produce variety within a coherent form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design the central architecture: protagonist, desire, obstacles, consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing story asks who these characters are, what they want, why they want it, how they attempt to get it, what stops them, and what the consequences are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At least 75% of the writer's labor should go into shaping these design questions. Use tools like spine, antagonism, turning points, progression, crisis, climax, subplots integrated into main plot. The craft of story is analytic as well as imaginative—map desires, actions, and causal consequences with rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid core story problems (false motivation, redundancy, holes, empty subtext)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common defects that kill stories include false motivation, redundant characters, empty or missing subtext, convenient coincidence, weak motivation, and unrelated tensions that never develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These flaws produce predictable, ill-told, clichéd episodes and an unengaging plot. Diagnose and remove convenient coincidences, ensure motivations are credible and character actions have logical and emotional cause, and make subplots meaningful and integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Values and meaning must be explicit and earned
rubrics_metrics.description: Story relies on a perception of values—what's worth living for, dying for, pursuing, or rejecting—and the writer must articulate this to an increasingly skeptical audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because modern audiences may not share assumed values, dig deeply into life to uncover fresh insights and refine values through the story. Use the narrative to explore and demonstrate ethical and emotional convictions rather than assuming them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn craft through study and apprenticeship
rubrics_metrics.description: Many writers rush into writing without studying the craft; fine screenwriting requires serious study and apprenticeship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study dramaturgy and story principles (intrinsic method: desire, antagonism, turning points, spine, progression, crisis, climax). Learn via university programs, libraries, theatre work, novels, apprenticeship, or mentorships. Avoid relying solely on casual film-watching or raw life experience as a substitute for disciplined learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary talent alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary talent—beautiful images, dialogue, and description—cannot substitute for true storytelling power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A photographically pretty or lyrically written script without progression, conflict, insight, or credible character design will not make a good film. Prioritize story design; dialogue and description are secondary and wasteful if they serve an 'anorexic yarn.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not call attention to the writer (avoid gimmicks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Never mistake eccentricity for originality; a mature artist never calls attention to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gimmicks, avant-garde quirkiness, or 'Look what I can do!' devices that draw attention away from story. Formal or stylistic stunts must serve the substance; otherwise they obstruct communication and weaken the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish to protect integrity on production
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfinished scripts invite tampering; polished, mature work seals its integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep rewriting until the script is director-ready and actor-ready. A well-crafted, thoroughly revised screenplay is less likely to be altered badly during production. Selling an immature first draft often leads to unwanted changes that damage the story.
